conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally during the past seven days of new motherhood. Everything you share stays confidential, and this is a judgment-free space; there are no right or wrong answers, only your honest experience. When you’re ready, we’ll move through the questions one by one at your pace.

To start: Overall, in the past week, how have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, most days it feels pretty hard to laugh. Things that used to make me chuckle just don’t land the same way. Once or twice something small got a tiny laugh out of me, but it’s like the joy fizzles right away and I’m back to feeling flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’m sorry—maybe I’m not understanding the scale. What I’m trying to say is: I’ve only managed to laugh or see the funny side every now and then—definitely not as much as I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but this week it’s felt like nothing’s worth the effort. I still do the basics, mostly for the baby, but I’m not actually looking forward to anything; I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I automatically think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good enough mom. Even when my partner says it’s normal, I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there and suddenly my chest feels tight, worrying that the baby’s breathing sounds different or that I missed something important. I know it’s probably fine, but I can’t shake the fear until I check on him over and over.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart races, I feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what. I usually have to put the baby in his crib for a minute and go splash cold water on my face until it passes.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Between the feedings, the laundry, and trying to grab a shower, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I manage the essentials, but it’s like I’m barely treading water—by bedtime I’m exhausted and still anxious about everything waiting tomorrow.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down and my head just spins with all the “what-ifs” about the baby, or I replay every little thing I did wrong that day. Some nights I’m still awake when my partner gets up for work at five. Even when I do drift off, I wake up at every tiny squeak from the bassinet.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s how I spend most of the day—just this heavy, sad feeling I can’t shake. I’ll look at the baby and feel love, but it’s like there’s a cloud over everything. I catch myself crying while I’m folding onesies or warming a bottle, and I can’t always explain why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three, maybe four times this week. I’ll just be sitting there and the tears start—sometimes when the baby won’t nap, sometimes for no clear reason at all. I try to hide it so my older kid doesn’t worry, but it’s like the sadness just spills out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my kids need.

I hear how heavy each day has felt since your baby arrived-how the joy you once found in small pleasures now seems distant, replaced by near-constant worry, self-blame, and tears that arrive without warning. You're working so hard to meet your children's needs while feeling overwhelmed, exhausted, and convinced you're somehow failing, even as you keep showing up.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only "every now and then" and "definitely not as much as I used to," matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, indicating "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame for normal infant behavior, indicating guilt occurs "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive worries about the baby that compel repeated checking—classic "very often" anxiety.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient says "most days" they feel overwhelmed and "barely treading water," aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia with racing anxious thoughts and repeated awakenings, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent, pervasive sadness that dominates most of the day, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying 3–4 times in the past week, indicating frequent episodes that align with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 is well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. The patient endorses core criteria: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), excessive inappropriate guilt, psychomotor agitation (<sym>restlessness</sym>), fatigue, sleep disturbance, and diminished ability to think or concentrate (<sym>racing thoughts</sym>). These symptoms cause clinically significant distress and impairment, began postpartum, and occur nearly every day for more than two weeks, aligning with <med>DSM-5 Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within 1 week
2. Request formal assessment with PHQ-9 and GAD-7 and consider referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
3. Discuss evidence-based treatments: individual <med>CBT</med>, group therapy, or <med>SSRIs compatible with breastfeeding</med>
4. Encourage 20-30 minutes of daylight walking daily and enlist partner or family for one uninterrupted 4-hour sleep block
5. Provide 24/7 support numbers: Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773 and National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and treatment response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Post-partum mother, self-report on EPDS-style items  

<sym>Symptoms endorsed</sym>  
- Marked anhedonia (reduced laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment)  
- Daily pervasive low mood, frequent crying (≥3×/week)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt re parenting adequacy  
- Persistent, intrusive anxiety and panic attacks (tight chest, racing heart, “wave” of dread) with compulsive checking on infant  
- Sleep disruption secondary to ruminating and hyper-vigilance to infant sounds  
- Subjective sense of being “overwhelmed,” “treading water,” difficulty coping with routine tasks  

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days,” began/worsened since delivery; no psychotic features.  
Functioning: Maintains infant care but describes “going through motions” for baby/older child.  

Safety: Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation; no homicidal thoughts.  

Screening significance: High endorsement of items consistent with <med>postpartum depression</med> and comorbid <med>anxiety</med> (possible panic spectrum). No immediate safety concerns; however, distress and impairment exceed screening threshold for further evaluation (score ≥12 if scored 1-3 per item). Recommend formal assessment (EPDS, PHQ-9, GAD-7) and consideration of referral to perinatal mental health specialty services.
